reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Amelia went to the library with her mother. She found a book about a red fire truck. The cover had words on it. "Those words say fire truck," said her mother. Amelia touched the letters. They were little and black.

She sat on a small green chair. She opened the book. "Start at the front," said her mother. Amelia turned one page. Then another. The fire truck went beep, beep! Amelia made the sound too. A boy nearby laughed.

At the desk, a lady scanned the book. "You can take it home," she said. Amelia hugged it tight.

At home, Amelia read the book four times. Then she put it under her pillow. "It sleeps with me," she said.

But the book had to go back. Other kids wanted to read it too. So on the last day, Amelia waved to the fire truck. "Bye, bye, truck," she said. At the library, she set it on the desk. Then she found a book about a big yellow bus.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Scarlett wanted to help Mom make soup. Mom said, "You can watch from here." Scarlett stood on her special stool, far from the stove. The pot went on the hot stove. Steam rose up. Steam looked soft, like a cloud. Scarlett reached out one finger. Mom caught her hand. "Steam is hot like the pot," Mom said. Scarlett pulled her hand back.

Then Mom gave her a job. "Put this cold spoon in the bowl." The spoon came from the fridge. It felt cool on Scarlett's fingers. She dropped it in the bowl. Clang! Mom poured the soup. The soup was too hot for Scarlett. Mom put the bowl on the windowsill. "We wait," said Mom. "Waiting keeps us safe."

Scarlett waited. She watched the steam go away, little by little. She touched the outside of the bowl. It was warm now, like her bed in the morning. Mom said, "All cool." Scarlett sat by Mom at the table. She took a small sip. It was just right. Mom smiled. Scarlett felt tired and happy. She rolled her spoon in the bowl, round and round.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Aubrey sat at the dinner table. Her tummy wanted the soup. But the soup was too hot. "Wait a bit," said Mom. Aubrey was lucky. She had five ways to check.

First, her eyes looked. She saw steam rise up. "I see steam," she said. Steam meant hot.

Next, her nose sniffed. She smelled carrots and warm bread. Then her ears listened. She heard the soup go pop, pop. Little bubbles jumped.

Aubrey put one finger near the bowl. Her skin felt the warm air. "Still hot," she said. Mom passed her the bread. "Try this first," said Mom.

Aubrey touched the bread. Warm, not hot. She took a little bite. Her tongue tasted salt and butter. "Yum," she said.

Aubrey counted on her fingers. "Eyes, nose, ears, hands, tongue. Five helpers!"

The steam went away. No more steam. Aubrey touched the bowl. Just right now. She tasted the soup. "Warm and good," she said. Mom smiled and gave her more.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Livia went to the art gallery with her mama. Big pictures hung on the walls. "I want to paint too," said Livia. "You can," said a kind lady named Rosa. Rosa had a paint table just for kids.

Rosa gave Livia three pots. "This one is red," said Livia. "This one is blue. This one is yellow!" Rosa smiled and nodded.

Livia dipped her brush in red. She made a big red circle. Then she dipped the same brush in blue. She painted next to the circle. "Oh no," said Livia. "The red followed the blue. Now it looks purple!"

Some paint dripped on the floor. A little boy almost stepped in it. "Watch out," said Livia. Rosa wiped the drip with a cloth. The wet cloth came away purple too. Livia laughed at the noise the brush made, swish, swish. She held up her painting for mama to see. "Look! Red and blue made purple!"

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Thomas wanted to wash his hands. He ran to the bathroom. Daddy came too.

Thomas saw two taps on the sink. He touched the cold tap. Cold water came out. Brrr! His hands felt icy.

Then he reached for the red tap. Daddy put his hand on top. "Let me," said Daddy. Daddy turned the red tap a little. Warm steam floated up. Thomas held his hand near it. Warm, but too hot for a little boy.

"I want to do it," said Thomas. Daddy turned the red tap off. Thomas turned the cold tap himself. He got lots of soap bubbles.

Afterward, Daddy dried Thomas's hands with the rough blue towel. "Don't forget your cookie," said Daddy. Thomas smiled. He ran to the kitchen with clean, warm hands.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Nora wanted to play outside in the snow. But first she needed her coat. She found it on the hook. It was red and soft like a sheep.

"One arm," said Nora. She pushed her arm in. "Two arms." She pushed the other arm in. Now the coat was on. But the zipper was stuck. Nora pulled it. It would not move. She pulled again, and the zipper made a loud zzzzzip sound. It went up a little! She pulled some more. Zzzzip. The coat closed all the way to her chin. Warm air stayed inside the coat.

Nora ran to the window. Mommy was putting on her boots. "I did it myself!" said Nora. She opened the door and stomped into the snow.

story:
Miles went to the library with his mom. They rode the bus. The bus was not heavy to ride, but his bag felt heavy. Miles wanted to draw a cat on the big tablet.

Miss Amy, the librarian, showed him the little round button. Miles pushed it. The screen lit up. He tapped the drawing app. A white page appeared. Miles drew a cat with orange ears. Then he drew a dog too.

"My picture is gone," he said. He had tapped a red X. Miss Amy showed him the back arrow. He tapped it. His cat came back. "It was hiding," said Miles. He laughed. When he was done, he pushed the button again. The screen went dark. He helped hang the tablet on its charging hook. "All done," he said. "Bye bye, cat."

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Cooper wanted to play with the big red truck. His sister Mia had it first. She pushed it across the floor. Cooper grabbed the truck. Mia began to cry.

Mom came in from the rain. Her umbrella was wet. "Let's try again," she said. She held up the truck. "First Mia. Then Cooper." Mia pushed the truck once. Then she gave it to Cooper. Cooper pushed it far under the table. He gave it back to Mia. The truck went back and forth. Both of them laughed.

Later they drew at the table. There was one blue crayon. Cooper wanted it. Mia held it out to him. "Your turn," she said. Cooper drew a big wet street with puddles. Then he gave the crayon back. Mia drew the rain.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Sara went to the library with her dad. She was excited. "Books!" she said.

Sara saw a boy crying by the shelves. His face was sad. He had lost his teddy bear. Sara looked under a table. No bear. She looked by the big chair. There it was! She ran and got it. The boy stopped crying. He smiled a big, happy smile. "Thank you," he told Sara.

Then a big book fell with a loud bang. Sara jumped. She felt scared. She held her dad's hand. Dad gave her a hug. Soon she felt better.

At the desk, a girl was angry. She wanted the last dinosaur book, but it was gone. Sara found a tiger book on the returns cart. The book had a wild tiger with big teeth. "Here," Sara said. The girl's face went soft. She smiled. "A wild tiger!" she said.

Sara picked three books for herself. Dad read them to her on the soft rug. Sara turned the last page and said, "Can we come back tomorrow?"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story: Declan ran to the little window at daycare. Yesterday, he had planted a seed in a cup. Today, the cup sat on the sunny sill. But the dirt looked the same. "Where is my plant?" Declan asked. Miss Rosa smiled. "It is not time yet. The seed sleeps now. It wakes up later." Declan touched the dirt. It was soft and damp. He gave the seed more water from a small cup. The water went down, down, down. Then he stuck a paper sun on the window. "Now the seed has two suns," he said. Miss Rosa laughed. "Come back tomorrow, Declan. Tomorrow will be different." Declan clapped his hands. He would wait. After nap time, he looked again. Still just dirt. But tomorrow was coming, and tomorrow, his plant might peek out.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Charlie wanted to make her own breakfast like a big girl. Daddy put warm toast on her plate. He put the butter dish next to it. Charlie held the butter knife in her hand.

"What does the butter do?" she asked. Daddy said, "Try it and look." Charlie pushed the cold butter. It stayed in a lump. Then she pushed the soft butter on the warm toast. It went smooth and shiny. The warm toast made the butter soft! "One, two, three," said Charlie, counting her strokes. The butter spread out thin, like a blanket on the toast.

Next came the milk. Charlie lifted the jug. It was heavy. The milk splashed over the edge of the cup. "Oh no," said Charlie. She looked at the puddle on the table. She wiped it up with a towel.

Then she tried again, slowly. "One, two, three," she said, counting the cup filling up. The milk stayed inside. Charlie took a bite of her toast. "Look, Daddy! A flower!" she said, pointing at the picture on his mug. Daddy smiled and poured one more cup, just for her.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Today was Madeline's birthday. Grandma's house smelled like cake. Big cousins ran by with balloons. Madeline wanted to blow out the candles. But the candles were not on the cake yet.

Grandpa carried the cake out slow. He set it on the table. The candles were not lit. "Wait," said Grandma. She struck one match. One candle lit. Then she touched it to each wick. The little flame made each candle light up, one by one. Madeline watched. One small fire made many candles burn.

"Now sit in your chair," said Daddy. Madeline sat. Everyone began to sing. Her voice felt warm inside. She took a big breath and blew. All the candles went out. Smoke curled up like thin gray ribbons. The candles felt cool when Daddy cut the cake near them.

Madeline got the first slice. It was chocolate, her favorite. Her friend Ben clapped for her. Madeline licked the frosting off her fork and grinned. "Happy birthday, Madeline!" everyone called. She waved her fork like a little flag.

story:
Maria put on her new hat. She ran to the backyard. "I will find something!" she said.

Her grandma sat on the step. "Stay where I can see you," said Grandma. Maria stayed close. She saw the grill. It was hot. The air above it wiggled. Grandma held a long fork. She did not let Maria touch.

Maria saw a shiny tool on the grass. She reached for it. "Not that one," said Grandma. "It is sharp." Grandma picked it up and put it far away.

Maria touched the cold birdbath instead. The water felt cool on her fingers. She touched her hat. The hat was warm from the sun. "This is warm," said Maria. "The water is cold."

Grandma smiled. "Come sit with me," she said. Maria wiped her wet hands on her dress. She sat by Grandma on the step. They watched a bird hop and drink.

"Stay close," said Grandma. Maria stayed close. The sun went down slow. The bird flew away. "Good night, bird," said Maria, waving her new hat.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Alice went to the store with her brother. He was hungry for apples. Mom said, "We need ten apples."

Alice held the bag. Mom put in one apple. Then two apples. Then three. The bag felt a little heavy.

"Can I try?" Alice asked. Mom smiled and gave her an apple. Alice counted, "Four, five, six." The bag got heavier and heavier. Each apple she added made the bag sag down.

"Seven, eight, nine," said her brother. He dropped in an apple too. Alice laughed. "Ten!" she said. The bag was too heavy to lift with one hand.

Mom held the big bag. Alice held her brother's hand. They walked to the apples one more time, because Alice wanted to count again. "One, two, three," she said.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Lydia went to the big game with Dad. They sat with Gran and her friend Tom. Lydia wanted to clap like everyone else.

The crowd began to cheer. Lydia clapped her hands. The claps made a big sound. But then everyone stopped, and her claps were small. "Too little," said Lydia.

Then Tom stood up. He waved his hands high. Lydia stood up too. She waved her hands high. Now the waves were big! Dad waved. Gran waved. One wave, two waves, three waves, all together.

The players looked up. They saw the waving crowd. They smiled and waved back. Lydia skipped in a little circle. Her tummy felt jumpy and happy. "We did that!" she said. Tom laughed and clapped for her. "Lydia wins the waving game," said Gran. Lydia waved one last big wave. The players waved back again.

story:
Emilia went to the store with Dad. She wanted a red balloon for Ben's present. But a boy was at the balloon stand first. He pointed at the red balloon too.

Emilia waited. She held Dad's hand and counted the balloons. There were ten. The man gave the boy the red balloon. Then the man pulled a new red balloon from the deep, deep box. It grew big and round.

The boy looked back at Emilia. He saw her sad face. He walked over with his balloon. "You can have this one," he said. "I will take a blue one." Emilia smiled. "Thank you," she said. "Blue is my next favorite." The man gave the boy a blue balloon. Emilia held her red balloon all the way to the party.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Chloe wanted to help Grandma bake cookies. "First, you must pass the sense test," said Grandma. "Five senses, five body parts. Can you name them?"

Chloe looked around the kitchen. She heard a buzzing sound. It came from the mixer! "Ears hear," said Chloe. "My ears heard the mixer!"

Grandma held up a lemon. "Close your eyes," she said. Chloe sniffed the lemon. Her nose wrinkled. "Yuck! My nose smells it!"

Grandma gave Chloe a crunchy apple slice. Crunch, crunch, crunch. "My mouth tastes," said Chloe, chewing. "And my mouth feels crunchy things too!"

"Now stop," said Grandma. She put the cookies in the oven. "Stay back, it is hot. What do your eyes do?"

"My eyes see the cookies!" said Chloe. She pressed her hands on the warm counter edge. "And my hands feel warm!"

"That is five," said Grandma. "Ears, nose, mouth, eyes, hands. You passed!"

Chloe clapped. "Can I taste the test again tomorrow?"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Andrew was a shy boy at the lake pool. He held the wall with both hands. "Come kick with me," said Dad. Andrew did not let go.

Dad held Andrew's tummy. "Kick your legs," said Dad. Andrew kicked one foot. Then he kicked the other. Little bubbles popped by his toes. Andrew kicked more. The bubbles popped faster. And then Andrew moved! He moved forward in the water. He kicked and kicked, all the way to Dad's arms.

"I did it!" said Andrew. "You did," said Dad. They tried again. And again. Andrew kicked and moved, slow and steady. Soon his eyes were sleepy. They sat in the sun on a big towel. "Nap time," said Dad. Andrew yawned. He watched the water sparkle, and he closed his eyes.

story: Chloe wanted toast like a big girl. Daddy made the toast, because the toaster was hot and not for little hands. Then he gave Chloe a dull little knife and soft butter. Chloe pressed the butter on the toast. It made a hole. "Oops," said Chloe. Daddy laughed. "Try little bits." Chloe took little bits. She slid the knife slowly. The butter spread like a soft, warm blanket. "Look at my blanket!" said Chloe. "Very cozy toast," said Daddy. Now Chloe wanted milk in her cup. She held the cup with one hand and the little jug with the other. She poured too fast. Milk ran down the side like a small, stormy river. Daddy wiped it up. "Slow hands," he said. Chloe poured again, very slowly. This time the milk went into the cup, not past it. Not one drop slipped away. Chloe clapped. Then she took a big bite of toast and a big sip of milk. "All by myself," she said, with a milk smile on her face.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Emilia held her bear tight. Today she would get a shot! She stood in the line with Mom. A girl ahead cried a little. Emilia's tummy felt weak.

"Will it hurt?" she asked.

"Just a tiny pinch," said Mom. "Then it is done."

The nurse smiled. "Squeeze your bear really hard," she said. Emilia counted, "One, two, three!" She squeezed with all her might. Then the nurse said, "All done!" Emilia looked down. The shot was over! She had not even felt it. Squeezing hard had made the pinch seem tiny.

The nurse put a bandage on Emilia's arm. It had little stars on it. Emilia held up her arm for everyone in the line to see.

"Look at my stars!" she said.

story:
Henry ran to the park. He wanted to find something new. His eyes saw a big red truck. The truck was digging a hole!

Henry listened with his ears. The truck went rumble, rumble. It was very loud. Henry put his hands over his ears. Then the truck stopped digging. The loud sound stopped too. Henry took his hands down. "It talks when it digs!" said Henry.

Henry smelled something with his nose. It was popcorn! Dad said, "We can buy some." Henry touched the warm bag with his fingers. It felt bumpy and warm. Henry took one piece and put it in his mouth. It tasted salty and yummy. A dog ran by. It was a smelly dog, but it was friendly. Henry patted its soft fur.

"Dad, my nose found the popcorn!" said Henry. Dad laughed and gave him one more piece.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Henry went to the library today. Yesterday the library had been closed. Henry had felt sad about that. But today the big doors were open.

"Story time is now," said the librarian, Miss Rose. Henry sat down on a soft red mat. He heard a story about a bear who baked a cake. The bear let a rabbit lick the spoon. Henry laughed at that part.

Then Henry found a book with a fire truck. "Can I take it home?" he asked. "Yes," said Miss Rose. "Bring it back tomorrow." Henry hugged the book tight.

"Is tomorrow soon?" Henry asked his mama. "Later," she said. "First we go home. Then we eat lunch. Tomorrow we come back." Henry looked out the window. The sun was up now. Tomorrow the sun would come up again.

At home, Henry put the book by his bed. "Read it now?" he asked. Mama read it two times. Henry patted the last page. "Again tomorrow," he said. Mama smiled and turned off the light.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Hayden went to the library with Mom. He wanted a book about elephants. The library was big and quiet.

He found a shelf with toy books. One book had a red fire truck. One book had a bouncy ball. Then he found a shelf with animal books. A big blue elephant smiled on the cover. "There he is!" Hayden whispered.

He pulled the elephant book out. A whole row of books leaned. They wobbled. "Oh no," said Hayden. He pushed the book back in. The row stood straight again. Books have their own home, just like animals and toys and foods.

He put the book under his arm. It felt a little loose, so he hugged it close. At the desk, the librarian stamped it. "Roar," said Hayden, very softly. The librarian winked and stamped her own hand too.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
story:
Lincoln pulled off his coat at the corner store. On the shelf sat two baskets of apples. One basket had a red sign. One basket had a green sign.

Linlin wanted to buy the basket with more apples. But which one had more? He counted the red basket. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six apples! Then he counted the green basket. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven apples. Seven was more than six.

But wait. What if he counted wrong? He touched the red apples again. This time he started from the other end. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Still six! He smiled a big smile. The last number was six both times. So the green basket really had more.

Lincoln carried the green basket to the counter. "Seven apples, please," he said. The apples smelled sweet, like the inside of a pie.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
The hall was big and noisy. Joshua sat at a long table with Grandma. Outside the window, the sky was cloudy. A dog outside began to bark. "Woof, woof!" said Joshua. Grandma laughed. "That dog is hungry too."

Big bowls of warm rice came to the table. Joshua grabbed his spoon right away. "Wait," said Grandma. "We say our words first." Grandma put her hands together. Joshua put his hands together too. "Thank you for our food," Grandma said slowly. "Thank you for our food," said Joshua.

Then Grandma picked up her spoon. Everyone at the table picked up a spoon. Joshua picked up his spoon too. "You said the words, so we eat!" said Uncle Ben. He took a big bite of rice. Joshua took a big bite too. "Again tomorrow?" asked Joshua. "Again tomorrow," said Grandma, and she winked.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Anna went to the playground with her red lion toy. The lion wanted to go on the big slide. Anna held him up high. "Slide with me, lion," she said.

A boy was standing at the slide. Anna wanted a turn too. "Can I have a turn, please?" she asked. The boy smiled and moved over. "Yes! You can go first." Anna sat down. Whoosh! Down she went, with the lion in her lap. "Thank you!" she called. "You're welcome," said the boy.

Next Anna wanted to climb the wall. It was too tall for her. "Can you help me, Mama?" she asked. Mama held her hand. Anna climbed up, up, up. From the top, Anna could see the whole playground. It was getting dark in the shade under the big tree.

Anna ran to the sandbox. Oops! She bumped into a girl. The girl dropped her bucket. "Sorry," said Anna. She picked up the bucket and gave it back. "It's okay," said the girl. "Want to make a castle?" Anna put her lion in the sand. "Yes, please!" she said. The lion sat on top of the castle like a king.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
William was at the festival with Grandma. There was a big long table. Lots of people sat at it. William was hungry. He wanted to eat the warm bread right away.

"Wait," said Grandma. "We say our word first." She put her hands together. So William put his hands together too. He said his word, small and quiet. Nobody heard him. His face felt warm and he looked down at the playground far away.

"Try again, one more time," said Grandma. William took a big breath. He said his word again, loud and clear. The people at the table heard him. They smiled and said it back to him. Then everyone ate the warm bread together. William took a big bite. Grandma gave him a thumbs up. "Again tomorrow?" she asked. William nodded, with bread still in his cheeks.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Blake walked on the nature trail with Gran. She wanted to play a game called Five Senses. But she did not know them all yet.

"Let's find them one by one," said Gran. Blake heard a bird. "That is hearing," she said. "My ears hear it!" Then she smelled a flower. "My nose smells it!" She touched a smooth rock. "My hands feel it!" She looked at a green leaf. "My eyes see it!"

One sense was left. Blake did not know it. Gran poured water from a bottle onto a berry bush. Little drops fell like rain. "Look how neat," said Gran. Blake stuck out her tongue. A drop landed on it. "My tongue tastes water!" she said. "That is the fifth one!" She counted her senses on her fingers, all the way to five.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Axel ran into his classroom. Snow was falling outside the window. It made a thick white blanket on the fence.

"Today we sing the counting song," said Miss Kim. "I need ten friends in a line."

Axel jumped up. He loved the counting song. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!

Miss Kim tapped each head. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine." Then she stopped. "We are one short."

Axel looked around. Mia was at the art table. "Mia, come quick!" he called. "We need you!"

Mia ran over and stood next to Axel. Miss Kim tapped her head. "Ten! Now we can sing."

The line sang loud. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Axel clapped at the end.

"Why did we need ten?" Mia asked.

Axel grinned. "Because Miss Kim taps one head for each number. Nine friends, then you!"

Miss Kim laughed. "Let's sing it again," she said. "Ten times fast!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Michael ran into Grandma's house. Tonight was Hanukkah! He wanted to see the candles.

Grandpa set the menorah on the table. Michael gave it a good spot near the window. Then Grandpa struck the match. Michael stayed back, just like Grandma said.

The flame touched the first wick. It lit up! The flame touched the second wick. That one lit too. But the last candle did not light. It was crooked. Its wick was too far away.

"The candle is crooked," said Michael. "The flame can't reach it!"

Grandpa pushed the candle straight. Then the flame touched the wick. Bright!

Michael clapped. All the candles shone now. The family sang songs. Michael sang loud. He spun the dreidel and won.

After, the dog, Grandma's pet, flopped by his feet. Michael was sleepy. He watched the candles glow and glow.

"Good night, candles," he whispered.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Bennett buckled into his car seat. "Are we almost there?" he called. "Almost!" said Dad. They were going to get ice cream. Big news! The best news!

Bennett looked out the window. A big truck went by. It was slow. A little red car zoomed past. It was fast. "Go, little car, go!" said Bennett. The sun came in through the glass. The sun made his arm warm. "My arm is hot!" he said. Dad turned the air on. Cool air blew on his face. "Cold air!" said Bennett. He laughed and laughed.

At the ice cream shop, Dad ordered two cones. One cone was big. It was for Dad. One cone was small. It was for Bennett. The ice cream was cold on his tongue. It was yummy, yummy, yummy. Bennett saw the sun shine on Dad's cone. Drip, drip, drip. It melted fast. His little cone stayed cold in the shade. Bennett held his cone up high. "My small one wins!" he called. Dad licked and licked his melting cone. "Yummy anyway," said Dad. Bennett took one big, happy bite.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma was coming to stay for a week. Violet wanted her room to feel like home. But Grandma looked sad at the table. "I miss my tea at my own house," Grandma said. Dad said, "I will make tea now." Violet watched Dad fill the kettle. Dad held the hot cup and set it down. "Careful, it is hot," Dad said. Violet stayed back.

Then the window turned white with fog. The hot tea made the glass fog up. Violet touched it with one finger. She drew a big round sheep. The fog held the shape. "That is funny," said Grandma. Grandma drew a little lamb next to it. Violet drew grass under the sheep. Grandma laughed and laughed. "My kitchen at home has a foggy window too," Grandma said. All week, they drew a new sheep every morning. On the last day, the whole window was full of sheep. Grandma hugged Violet tight. "Same time tomorrow," Grandma said, and tapped the glass.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Andrew went to the park with his dad. He wanted to slide down the big slide. He held his dad's hand all the way there.

Near the slide, Andrew saw a metal grill. It was hot. Dad said, "Stand back, buddy." Andrew saw steam rise from it. He felt warm air on his face, even from far away. He put his hands behind his back and watched.

A small dog ran by with a shiny can in its mouth. Andrew wanted to grab it. The can had sharp edges. Dad knelt down and said, "That could cut you. Let it be." Andrew nodded. He kept walking.

Then he reached the slide. He climbed up, up, up. He sat down and let go. Whee! He slid down fast and landed on the snowy cold ground. "Brrr!" said Andrew. Dad laughed and held out his mittens.

"One more time?" asked Andrew. "You got it," said Dad.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Blake went to the library with her dad. She saw a new puzzle on the low table. It had a picture of a blue lake with ducks on it. A boy named Sam was already playing with it.

Blake wanted the puzzle too. She grabbed a duck piece. Sam held on tight. The piece would not move at all.

"Can we both play?" Blake asked.

"Yes," said Sam. "You do the sky. I do the lake."

Blake put in the sky pieces. Sam put in the ducks. Then they traded, and Blake got the ducks. The puzzle got bigger and bigger. When it was done, the whole lake shone blue.

"We win!" said Sam. Blake clapped her hands.

Then Blake picked up a book about ducks. She sat down next to Sam on the little carpet. "Do you want to look too?" she asked.

"Yes, please," said Sam. They turned the pages together, one at a time.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Iris wanted to wear her red shoe. But it was not on her feet. It was not by the door. "Where did it go?" she asked. "Yesterday you wore it in the jam," said Mom. "It got sticky." So Mom washed the shoe. Then she set it on the shelf to dry.

"Now we wait," said Mom. Iris touched the shoe. It was still wet. "Not now," said Mom. "Later it will be dry." Iris looked at her toes. They wiggled in the dark. She wiggled them again. "My toes tickle me," she said. Mom laughed.

Iris put on her slippers. She brushed her teeth. She picked two books, not three. Mom read them slow. Then Iris looked at the shelf one more time. The shoe sat there, quiet and wet.

"In the morning it will be dry," said Mom. "Tomorrow you can wear it." Iris got in bed. She pulled the blanket up high. Tomorrow felt like a long way off. But tomorrow would come after sleep. Iris closed her eyes. She thought about her red shoe, waiting on the shelf. "Goodnight, shoe," she whispered. "See you tomorrow."

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Oliver sat at the picnic table at camp. He was making a lion mask from a paper plate. Miss Ana had cut two holes for eyes. Oliver painted the plate yellow with a big brush.

Then he wanted to add an orange mane. He squeezed lots of glue around the edge. He stuck on orange paper strips one by one. But the glue was wet and shiny. A strip slid off the plate and onto the table.

"Why does my mane keep falling off?" Oliver asked. Miss Ana smiled. "The glue is still wet. Wet glue is slippery. It cannot hold the paper yet."

So Oliver put the strips back. He pressed each one with his palm. Then Miss Ana carried the mask to a sunny bench. "The sun will help," she said. Oliver watched. The glue went from shiny to dull. Soon it was dry. Dry glue held the strips tight.

Oliver picked up the mask. He pulled one strip gently. It did not move. "My mane is stuck on!" he said. He put the mask on his face. He gave a big roar. Then his friend Mia came over, holding a plain white plate. She looked sad. Her paint had spilled.

Oliver ran to the craft box. He came back with his yellow paint pot. "You can share mine," he said. Mia dipped her brush. She painted a sun on her plate. Then she pointed at Oliver. "Roar again," she said. Oliver lifted his lion head and roared.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Brielle stood in the reading corner. It had a soft red rug and a shelf full of books. She wiggled her toe in her sock and smiled.

"Today you get your own library card," said Mom. "Then you can pick a book."

Brielle picked a book about a big yellow truck. The librarian put the book in a bag. "You can take it home," she said. "Bring it back in one week."

"One week is very long," said Brielle. "I want to keep the truck book forever."

Mom shook her head. "The book belongs here. Other kids want to read it too."

Brielle held the bag tight. She did not want to let it go. Then she saw a boy by the shelf. He was looking for a truck book. There were no more truck books on the shelf.

Brielle looked at her bag. Then she looked at the boy. She gave the book to the librarian. "He can have it first," she said.

The boy smiled big. "Thank you," he said.

The librarian stamped a paper. "You can have it after him," she told Brielle. Brielle put the paper in her pocket.

"Can we come back next week?" she asked Mom.

"Yes," said Mom. "And we will read it two times."

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Aiden ran to the park with his red balloon. The sun did shine on the big slide. Aiden felt excited. He held the balloon string tight.

A little girl was on the swing. She looked sad. Her ice cream had dropped on the ground. Aiden watched the ice cream drip down. The girl began to cry. Aiden felt sad too.

Then a big dog ran by. The dog jumped up. Its nose hit the balloon. Pop! The balloon was gone. Aiden felt angry. He stamped his foot. Then he felt a little scared, because the dog was big.

But the dog licked his hand. It was a friendly dog. Aiden laughed and patted its soft ears. The sad girl came over. She laughed too. The dog's tail wagged far and wide. Aiden felt happy again.

The girl's mom gave them each a new ice cream. The three friends sat on the warm bench. The dog rested at their feet. "Good dog," said Aiden, and the dog wagged some more.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Matteo wanted to help bake bread at daycare. Miss Ana said, "You can help mix." Matteo touched the dough with his fingers. It was soft and squishy. He poked it. It made a little dent. Then the dent went away. How did that happen? The dough was stretchy, so it came back.

Miss Ana let Matteo smell the flour. It smelled like nothing much. But soon the bread went into the big oven. Miss Ana put it in, because the oven could burn little hands. Matteo stayed back and watched. Then a warm smell filled the room. Matteo sniffed with his nose. "What is that smell?" he asked. "It is our bread," said Miss Ana. Could a smell tell him something? Yes, it could.

The bell went ding. Matteo heard it with his ears. The bread was ready. Miss Ana cut one short piece for each child. Matteo tasted his piece. It was warm and good on his tongue. Outside, they ate snack on a small hill of grass. The bread was gone, but the smell still sat in Matteo's nose. "Again tomorrow?" he asked. "Again tomorrow," said Miss Ana, and she held up the empty bowl.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Beatrice went to Grandma's house in the morning. Grandma had a big piano in the front room. Beatrice wanted to play a song all by herself.

She pressed one key. It made a low sound, boom. She pressed another key. It made a high sound, ding. One key, one sound. Two keys, two sounds.

"Grandma, can I make three sounds?" asked Beatrice. Grandma smiled. "Press three keys, one by one." Beatrice pressed one, two, three. Ding, ding, boom! The sleepy cat sat up and opened her eyes.

Beatrice played the keys fast. The cat's tail began to swish. Beatrice played the keys slow. The cat's tail went still and soft. Fast keys made the tail fly up. Slow keys made the tail rest down.

Beatrice laughed. She played a slow song for the sleepy cat. The cat walked over and curled up on the piano bench. "Good morning, cat," said Beatrice. She played one more soft key, ding.
